IHG unveils six-bedroom villa in Vietnam and first Kimpton hotel in Indonesia
article:
IHG Hotels & Resorts is adding new luxury accommodation in Vietnam and Indonesia, with the launch of an ultra-exclusive, six-bedroom beachfront villa at InterContinental Halong Bay Resort and the upcoming opening of Kimpton Suntaya Bali Ubud later this year.

The villa, known as the Halong Bay Estate, is the latest addition to InterContinental Halong Bay Resort, which opened in 2025 overlooking the world-renowned bay with emerald waters and limestone islands.

Meanwhile, the 101 -key Kimpton Suntaya Bali Ubud will mark the Kimpton brand’s debut in Indonesia.

Looking to invest in overseas properties ? Explore projects available for sale around the world

A six-bedroom estate overlooking Ha Long Bay

Positioned directly along the resort’s sandy beachfront, the Halong Bay Estate spans 565 sq m (6,082 sq ft) and is designed for families, groups, corporate retreats and private celebrations.

The sprawling six-bedroom villa has multiple living and entertainment areas, including a private cinema, billiard room, library, gym, spa and sauna. Its sea-facing outdoor spaces include open-air terraces and an infinity pool overlooking Ha Long Bay.

Rates start from US$9,600 (S$12,323.90) per night, inclusive of daily breakfast.

Guests will also have access to a private chef, with breakfast, afternoon tea and evening cocktails served within the villa.

The estate forms part of InterContinental Halong Bay Resort, a beachfront development comprising 174 guestrooms and suites, 60 residences and 41 private villas. The accommodation overlooks Ha Long Bay, a Unesco World Heritage Site.

Elsewhere in the resort, guests have access to three swimming pools, the Hidden Lagoon Spa, a yoga area, fitness centre, cinema room and Planet Trekkers children’s activity centre. The property also has more than 4,500 sq m of indoor and outdoor event space, including the Tonkin Ballroom.

Grant Thompson, general manager of InterContinental Halong Bay Resort, says the new villa is intended to encourage travellers to spend more time at the destination rather than visiting only as part of a short cruise trip.

“We are positioning Ha Long Bay not only as part of an itinerary, but as a standalone destination,” he says.

The resort has also introduced Yulong Mansion, a Cantonese restaurant led by head chef Kan, and appointed former Nobu executive chef Andy Huynh to lead Roku, its Japanese restaurant and sky bar.

Kimpton to make its Indonesia debut in Ubud

In Indonesia, IHG is set to debut Kimpton Suntaya Bali Ubud later this year.

Located along Jalan Bisma, the hotel is a short walk from Ubud Art Market, Ubud Palace and the Water Palace.

The property will offer 101 rooms, pool suites and private pool villas. Set beside the Wos River, it is designed to follow the contours of Ubud’s hillside and riverside landscape.

Architecture firm Denton Corker Marshall conceived the property as a contemporary interpretation of Balinese ceremonial processions. Its buildings are arranged as a layered composition across the site, while the façade and structural rhythm draw from the movement and collective energy associated with local ceremonies.

Facilities will include five dining venues, a two-storey fitness studio, recovery facilities and a spa which takes inspiration from Balinese healing traditions. Austin Jones, general manager of Kimpton Suntaya Bali Ubud, says: “Kimpton Suntaya is designed to feel open, soulful, and connected, not just to the landscape, but to the people who live and travel here.”

title: Owners of Lakeside Towers hope for third-time-lucky $350 mil en bloc sale
article:
The owners of Lakeside Towers are hopeful that they will be third time lucky in their latest collective sale attempt. The 144-unit development has secured the consent of over 80% of the owners to launch the collective sale at the reserve price of $350 million.

The 153,237 sq ft site is zoned "residential" with a base gross plot ratio (GPR) of 2.1. Under the 2025 Master Plan, the site has an as-built gross plot ratio of 2.36.

After factoring in an estimated lease top-up premium and bonus gross floor area (GFA) for balconies — with no land betterment charge payable — the reserve price translates to a land rate of $1,277 psf per plot ratio (psf ppr), says Nicholas Ng, JLL Singapore head of land and collective sales, who is handling the sale.

Assuming an average size of 85 sq m (915 sq ft), the new development could yield 395 units, estimates Ng.

The existing development has two 20-storey blocks on a site with a 190m frontage of Jurong Lake Gardens. It is also the last site along Yuan Ching Road where residents have direct frontage and access to Jurong Lake Gardens.

‘Dragon's head’

“The residents call the site ‘the dragon’s head’,” says Ng. He attributes it to the location.

The residents are well-served by sports facilities, including Jurong East Sports Centre, SuperBowl Jurong, SAFRA Jurong, and the ActiveSG sports village at Jurong Town .

That's why Maureen Tan, the collective sale committee (CSC) chairwoman, and her husband chose Lakeside Towers as their new home six years ago. Their previous home was a Black & White (B&W) conserved property at Woodleigh Park, which they rented from the Singapore Land Authority (SLA).

The couple were considering whether to rent another B&W property when they chanced upon an apartment at Lakeside Towers that was offered for sale then. "My husband loves the Jurong Lake Gardens, the outdoors, and enjoys walking and cycling in the park,” she says. “There is also the ActiveSG gym at Jurong West Sports Centre just down the road."

Spanning 90ha, Jurong Lake Gardens is Singapore's first national garden in the suburbs. The other two national gardens are the 101ha Gardens by the Bay and the 82ha Singapore Botanic Gardens.

In 2014, it was announced that the Chinese and Japanese Gardens, both built in the mid-1970s, would be combined with Jurong Lake Park (now known as Lakeside Garden) to create Jurong Lake Gardens.

Rejuvenation works by the National Parks Board began in 2019 to enhance both the Chinese and Japanese Gardens, and were completed five years later, with the gardens reopened in 2024.

Amenities in the area

Lakeside Towers is also just a 10-minute walk to the Lakeside MRT Station on the East-West Line. It's a pleasant walk as the path to the MRT station is sheltered by trees, adds Tan. Jurong East MRT interchange is just three stops away.

Schools located within 1km of Lakeside Towers include Lakeside Primary School and Shuqun Primary School. The Canadian International School is a short drive away via Boon Lay Way, adds Tan.

Malls nearby include JEM , Westgate , IMM, Taman Jurong Shopping Centre and Boon Lay Shopping Centre . Looking further ahead, the Singapore Tourism Board (STB) has announced longer-term plans for an integrated development in the Jurong Lake District, notes JLL's Ng.

The new Singapore Science Centre will be situated next to the Chinese Garden MRT station, just one MRT stop away. It is designed by Zaha Hadid Architects in collaboration with Architects 61, with Atelier Ten as the sustainability consultant. The development is targeted for completion by the end of 2027.

Last of three sites fronting Jurong Lake Gardens

According to JLL's Ng, there are three 99-year leasehold developments along Yuan Ching Road, of which Lakeside Towers is the last to be put up for sale. The first two have already been sold en bloc.

Next door to Lakeside Towers was the former Lakeside Apartments , which was sold en bloc to Wing Tai Holdings in May 2022 for $273.88 million ($1,250 to $1,260 psf ppr).

Wing Tai launched the new development on the site, the 306-unit LakeGarden Residences, in August 2023. To date, the project is 99% sold at an average price of $2,160 psf, based on caveats lodged.

On the other side of the upcoming LakeGarden Residences is the former Park View Mansions, which was purchased en bloc for $260 million ($1,023 psf ppr) by a consortium made up of SingHaiyi, KSH Holdings and Ho Lee Group in July 2022.

The new 440-unit private condo, Sora , was launched in July 2024. The project is 51% taken up at an average price of $2,237 psf.

CDL's Lucerne Grand to set new price benchmark

Meanwhile, City Developments Ltd (CDL) plans to launch its 570-unit Lucerne Grand private condo project on Lakeside Drive in 3Q2026. Located near Jurong Lake Gardens and beside Lakeside MRT Station, Lucerne Grand comprises five 17-storey towers with a commercial podium on the first storey.

CDL had clinched the Lakeside Drive site with the top bid of $608 million ($1,132 psf ppr) in a Government Land Sale (GLS) tender in June 2025. Back then, analysts had estimated that the average selling price of homes at the future development could hover around $2,400 psf and set a new price benchmark for the Lakeside area. Lucerne Grand stands to benefit from the upcoming Jurong Lake District, CDL said in its 1Q2026 operational update on May 20.

The future redevelopment of Lakeside Towers will benefit from the new amenities coming up in the Jurong Lake District, and from the launch of Lucerne Grand, says JLL's Ng.

Renewal of ageing neighbourhoods through collective sale

Lakeside Towers was built in 1981, which makes it 45 years old. It has a 99-year lease from 1975, which means a remaining lease of 48 years.

In a bid to support the renewal of ageing estates, the Ministry of Law has proposed lowering the consent thresholds for older developments to secure a collective sale under the Land Titles (Strata) (Amendment) Bill, tabled in Parliament on Aug 4. The threshold would fall from 80% to 70% for developments aged between 40 and 59 years, and to 65% for those aged 60 years and above.

However, Lakeside Towers already obtained the 80% agreement ahead of the amendments. Hence, it will not be affected by the latest amendments, says Ng.

"The owners are motivated to sell because of the depreciating lease," he adds. "When the project is redeveloped, it will help rejuvenate the neighbourhood."

The tender for Lakeside Towers closes on Thursday, October 1, at 3pm.

title: From Silicon Valley to Serangoon: 3 Semiconductor Stocks Riding the US Tech Wave
article:
When investors think about the
AI boom
, chip companies such as
NVIDIA Corporation
(NASDAQ: NVDA),
Broadcom Inc.
(NASDAQ: AVGO) and
Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.
(NASDAQ: AMD) usually come to mind.
But every AI chip that powers a data centre needs to be designed, manufactured, tested and assembled.
This is where Singapore comes in.
Semiconductor
production requires a global supply chain, and several SGX-listed companies play key roles.
Here are three of them.
Micro-Mechanics Holdings (SGX: 5DD) – The Precision Engineering Specialist
Micro-Mechanics has two main businesses.
First, it designs and manufactures tools for semiconductor packaging, assembly and testing processes.
Second, it manufactures precision components for critical production processes in wafer-fabrication equipment.
As such, rising wafer-fabrication activity should increase demand for products in both of Micro-Mechanics’ businesses.
This is already starting to show in its financials – revenue growth in the company’s most recent quarter (January to March 2026) accelerated to 16.2%, compared to a 14.5% increase in the previous quarter (October to December 2025).
Margins are also trending up, with operating profit as a percentage of revenue rising from 26% in the January to March 2025 quarter to 28% in the same period a year later.
These results are driven by over 600 customers worldwide, with the company’s top 10 customers primarily located in the US, China and Malaysia – these three markets contributed 72% of total revenue in its fiscal year ended 30 June 2025 (FY2025).
One customer of its wafer fabrication equipment parts segment represented nearly 10% of overall revenue for FY2025.
Although the semiconductor business has traditionally been a cyclical one, Micro-Mechanics is conservatively run, with nearly S$26 million in cash on its balance sheet and no borrowings in its most recent quarter.
The company’s share price was up 68.1% for the year to 28 July.
UMS Integration Limited (SGX: 558) – The Semiconductor Equipment Provider
UMS’s semiconductor business is focused on providing equipment manufacturing and engineering services to original equipment manufacturers of semiconductors, focusing on the initial stages of the wafer fabrication process, including areas such as photolithography, etching and deposition.
With its revenue down by 19% in 2024, UMS returned to top-line growth of 4% in 2025.
According to UMS, both of its key global customers are forecasting “robust” demand growth for 2026 and 2027, and expect multiple years of outperforming their targets going forward.
However, UMS has to invest to take advantage of this demand.
Free cash flow in 2025 fell to S$2 million from S$23 million the year before, because of an increase in inventories and higher capital expenditure to support its expansion in Penang, which is needed to ramp up future production.
UMS’s semiconductor business is concentrated – the segment had revenue of S$215 million in 2025, and more than 50% of this was from sales to its largest customer.
Both of the company’s key customers are “important players” in the semiconductor advanced packaging space, which will benefit from increasing demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips.
This concentration has benefits.
Exploding demand for HBM chips has sent UMS’s share price soaring.
As of 4 August 2026, its share price has doubled year-to-date, with a gain of 108.3%.
AEM Holdings (SGX: AWX) – The Testing and Manufacturing Solutions Provider
AEM provides the semiconductor and electronics sectors with test solutions.
AI chips are getting more complex, consuming more power, and have increasing application specificity.
These trends mean AI chips require new and more extensive testing methods.
To address these challenges, AEM’s technology enables customers to test a significantly larger number of devices simultaneously while maintaining precise and stable test conditions.
The company’s revenue in 2025 was driven by its Test Cell Solutions (TCS) segment, which accounted for 63% of overall revenue of S$399 million.
TCS grew by 8.8%, faster than total revenue growth of 5%.
Notably, TCS’s revenue growth is accelerating rapidly.
In the first quarter of 2026 (1Q2026), TCS revenue surged 72% year on year.
AEM’s bottom line is also soaring, with 1Q2026 earnings per share 337% higher than a year ago.
This has been reflected in AEM’s share price, which was almost five times higher year-to-date (as of 4 August 2026).
AEM’s business is relatively concentrated.
In 2025, one customer accounted for S$152 million in revenue, or 38% of overall sales.
Going forward, AEM expects its advanced thermal technologies, expertise in high-parallel test systems, and proprietary test instrumentation to continue setting it apart from competitors.
Risks Investors Should Watch
Before putting all their chips on the table, investors should note that the semiconductor industry has traditionally been highly cyclical.
Although many think that this AI-driven cycle is different, the recent sell-off in memory chip shares – which caused both UMS and AEM’s share prices to fall by over 8% on 28 July – is a reminder of the sector’s volatility.
One of the reasons for the sell-off was the fear that any delays in capital expenditure by the large hyperscalers may affect demand for chips, which will in turn reduce demand for the products and services of these Singapore semiconductor companies.
UMS and AEM, in particular, are also exposed to a greater degree of customer concentration risk, since both are dependent on just one customer each for a significant portion of their revenues.
Finally, elevated valuations leave less margin for error if demand disappoints.
These SGX-listed companies are trading at trailing 12-month price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios of 27.0x (Micro-Mechanics), 48.7x (UMS) and 154.4x (AEM) as at 4 August 2026.
Get Smart: You Don’t Need to Own Silicon Valley to Benefit from AI
The AI revolution extends well
beyond America’s largest technology companies
.
Singapore’s semiconductor ecosystem provides investors with exposure to one of the world’s strongest secular growth trends.
By focusing on quality businesses with strong industry positioning, investors can participate in the AI supply chain without necessarily buying the headline-grabbing
US technology
giants.

title: Investing in a K-shaped economy
article:
THERE has been a lot of chatter
about the K-shaped economy
.
A yawning gap exists between high earners who are spending and growing their wealth, and low-income households who have to live from hand to mouth.
The K-shaped economy may also be evident at the corporate level, in which rich companies expand rapidly, while smaller businesses struggle to pay their bills.
Many consumer-facing businesses have been highlighting what they see as a bifurcated economy.
Airlines, for instance, have talked about a growing demand for seats at the front of the plane, while some budget airlines have faced problems attracting passengers.
Fast-food restaurants have been forced to introduce more affordable items into their menus, while many fine-dining restaurants appear to be unaffected.
The K-shaped economy has not been lost on the US Federal Reserve.
Last year, it said many consumers at the lower end are struggling, and that they are buying less and shifting to lower-cost products.
At the top of the consumption pyramid, people are spending freely. How can an economy that is running piping hot at one end and stone cold on the other meet the needs of the people in the middle?
The shape of things to come
Could what we are witnessing be a delayed aftershock from COVID-19?
After the pandemic-induced economic slowdown, there was speculation that the recovery could be V, U, L or even W-shaped. But it is looking increasingly likely that the global economy is experiencing an awkward K-shaped recovery.
A V-shaped recovery implies that an economic downturn is followed by a sharp recovery.
In an U-shaped recovery, an economy bumps along the bottom for a while following a downturn, before it recovers sharply.
In an L-shaped recovery, an economy never fully gets back to its former glory. With a W-shaped recovery, an economy rebounds, then shrinks before recovering again.
But a K-shaped recovery can pose all kinds of problems.
At a superficial level, we may think that any economic recovery is better than no recovery at all. What is more, from a macroeconomic level, a country can even appear to be in quite good health.
But this can be masking some serious problems not only at the corporate level, but also at the social level.
This is because wealthier households are currently believed to be the main drivers of consumer spending. Less wealthy consumers, on the other hand, are struggling to survive; they are living from one pay cheque to another.
From top to bottom
The post-pandemic economic recovery is far from over, even though it has been a full six years.
Everything may appear to be fine when we look at the top-level gross domestic product numbers.
But they do not quite tell the whole story. As investors, we need to know which companies are on the upward stroke of the “K”, and which ones are struggling on the downward leg.
Some industries are clearly enjoying strong growth in output, while others are experiencing declining activity.
We have, for instance, seen some types of asset values rise, while others have fallen. Some segments of society are seeing increasing wealth and income, but others are losing ground.
Businesses, therefore, need to be more nuanced in dealing with growing income inequality. The smart ones are those that have worked out what a K-shaped recovery means for them, and how they can develop strategies that cater to both.
Effectively, what we are dealing with is economic growth and
recession
to the point of depression, simultaneously.
It is hard
Investing is easy if we know whether we are experiencing economic growth or recession. It is also easy for a central bank to implement monetary policy under those clear-cut conditions.
But it can be a lot harder when economic conditions are fuzzy.
Additionally, investing can become more complicated when new technologies such as artificial intelligence could upend older technologies and industries. It can even result in creative destruction within an economy.
The key to investing in these conditions is to admit that we just do not know what can happen.
We have no idea whether central banks will tighten monetary policy to rein in inflation, or sit on their hands because they are worried about recession.
Meanwhile, governments could put in place fiscal measures to ease the burden of long-suffering households, which can be inflationary.
Regardless of what may happen in global economies, it is important to
stay invested
for the long term.
Warren Buffett once said: “I’ve never bought a stock or sold a stock based on what the Fed is going to do. And if the Fed chairman should whisper in my ear exactly what he’s going to do tomorrow, it wouldn’t change anything I’m going to do today.”
Investing should never be about second-guessing what may happen.
I have no idea whether the K-shaped economy is real or a figment of some economist’s fertile imagination. I have no advanced knowledge of whether AI will be a peach of an investment or just another technological lemon.
For me, investment should be about buying a portfolio of diversified shares in good companies that will be able to
reward us over the long term
.
As an income investor, I am continually buying rising income – at a discount if I can, at a premium if I must. But I am always buying income in the knowledge that rising dividends is the best antidote to persistent inflation.
Central banks will do whatever they think is right for their economy. As private investors, we need to do what is right for us.
Say you have S$100,000 in a six-month T-bill. In 2023, that would’ve earned you over S$3,000. Today, at 1.4%, you’re looking at S$1,400. Same amount of money, half the income, while your grocery bill hasn’t gotten cheaper. Our webinar shows you where that S$100,000 could work harder.

title: China’s official newspaper warns US over expanding tech curbs
article:
(Aug 5): The official newspaper of China’s ruling Communist Party warned of countermeasures against widening US technology curbs as Washington considers banning imports of some Chinese AI components, adding a fresh source of strain to the countries’ fragile trade truce.

In a commentary published Wednesday, the People’s Daily accused the US of “unilateral bullying” over the Federal Communications Commission’s (FCC) announcement last week that it would tighten restrictions on some foreign-made robots and power inverters, sectors in which China is a dominant manufacturer.

The newspaper did not mention the proposed restrictions on data centre components reported Tuesday, but its warning underscored the potential for Washington’s growing campaign against Chinese technology to complicate efforts by Donald Trump and Xi Jinping to stabilise relations before the Chinese leader’s expected US visit next month.

“The US measures, under the pretext of ‘non-discrimination’ or ‘national security,’ are in essence discriminatory treatment and suppression targeting Chinese enterprises and products,” the newspaper said. The commentary was credited to Zhong Sheng, a Chinese homonym for “Voice of China” that’s often used to convey Beijing’s views on foreign policy.

The FCC is drafting an order to ban Chinese-made data centre components, Bloomberg reported Tuesday, citing a person familiar with the matter. Reuters reported earlier that the agency was considering barring imports of new models of Chinese optical transceivers, which enable data to move at high speeds within and between data centres.

The agency is also considering other steps to prevent blacklisted China-based companies from connecting to US networks, the House Select Committee on China said in a report on the same day. The committee found that regulatory gaps had allowed three Chinese telecommunications companies barred from directly connecting to US networks to retain links to America’s internet infrastructure.

Chinese optical-equipment stocks slid on Wednesday morning, with Zhongji Innolight Co falling as much as 14% in Shenzhen before paring the decline. US, European and Japanese suppliers rallied, suggesting investors expect the proposed restrictions to hurt Chinese companies while benefitting overseas rivals.

Chinese suppliers control more than half of the high-speed transceiver market, leaving major cloud-computing companies with few near-term alternatives and potentially setting up industry resistance that could soften the proposed policy, according to Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Sean Chen.

See also: Startup founder buys Washington bank to extend fintech push

Chinese companies may also be able to circumvent the restrictions by shipping products through factories in Southeast Asia, depending on how the FCC defines a Chinese optical transceiver, Chen said.

China exported US$61.6 million of optical transceivers to the US in June, accounting for 8.7% of its worldwide shipments. The US was previously the biggest destination for Chinese transceivers, but exports fell sharply after Trump returned to the White House last year.

Malaysia, where investment in data centres has surged, has since become the leading destination. It received US$260 million of Chinese optical-transceiver shipments in June.

Optical transceivers made up just 0.2% of China’s total exports in June, though shipments rose 27% from a year earlier in the first half.

The People’s Daily listed earlier FCC actions targeting Chinese telecommunications and video-surveillance equipment, drones and routers, describing them as part of an effort to suppress Chinese technology and contain the country’s industrial development.

“This move by the US side runs counter to the current momentum of stabilisation and improvement in China-US relations,” the newspaper said, citing the May summit in Beijing between Xi and Trump. “If the US side is bent on going its own way, China will take resolute countermeasures.”

title: Thailand rules out fully owned SpaceX venture in US trade talks
article:
(Aug 5): Thailand won’t allow US firms to establish fully foreign-owned satellite telecoms as part of trade talks with the Trump administration, resisting such investments in the sector over sovereignty issues, said the country’s vice-commerce minister.

The topic will be on the agenda when trade talks with Washington resume near the end of this month, Thailand Vice Commerce Minister Kirida Bhaopichitr said in an interview.

“There’s only one sector I think we actually would not want them to invest, which is the low-orbit telecommunication service,” she said. “That’s a sovereign issue. Basically, there’s only one company in the US that really wants this, which is SpaceX.”

The US Trade Representative and SpaceX didn’t respond to separate requests for comment.

Elon Musk’s satellite, space and artificial intelligence company, which went public in June, has been seeking greater access to offer Starlink satellite internet services in Thailand, where restrictions limit foreign ownership to 49% of some telecommunications infrastructure.

Thailand is committed to buying more American airplanes, liquefied natural gas, soybeans and corn, Kirida said. The country will also reduce tariffs to zero and accept US standards for imports of beef, lamb and alcohol. However, it won’t grant the same treatment for US pork, she said.

See also: World Bank urges emerging nations to embrace AI amid weak growth

Bangkok’s main goal with US trade talks is to keep total tariffs below the 19% rate it agreed to last year, she said, which it had before a US Supreme Court ruling overturned President Donald Trump’s trade playbook.

To restore Trump’s tariff leverage, the USTR has opened multiple so-called Section 301 investigations on what it considered unfair trade practices.

Thailand is already subject to a 12.5% tariff under a USTR ruling that hit 60 countries for not taking adequate steps to limit the trade of good produced using forced labour. It’s also subject to a separate ongoing investigation into excess production capacity.

See also: Vapes, liquor, soft drinks face higher taxes in Philippines

Thailand late last year rejected a SpaceX proposal to establish a 100% foreign-owned subsidiary, The Nation newspaper reported in November, citing Digital Economy Minister Chaichanok Chidchob.

title: China’s services gauge hits two-year low as firms turn cautious
article:
(Aug 5): China’s services activity expanded at its weakest pace in nearly two years, a private survey showed, with businesses turning more cautious about an economy that’s increasingly showing signs of further weakness.

The RatingDog China services purchasing managers’ index slipped to 50.4 from 54.1 in June, according to a statement published Wednesday. That fell far short of the median forecast of economists surveyed by Bloomberg but stayed above the 50 mark separating expansion from contraction.

The reading is the lowest since September 2024. It roughly tracked the official PMI survey, which showed the services industry slipped back into contraction last month for the first time since April, slumping the most in about two and a half years. Factory activity in July also slowed on adverse weather conditions and weak demand.

While the services gauge is expected to be in expansionary territory in the near term, the pace of the recovery will depend on the strength of domestic demand and business confidence, said RatingDog founder Yao Yu.

Business expectations for the year ahead, while still positive, have softened to the lowest since February 2020, he said in a statement. “Confidence was linked to business expansion plans, new projects and promotional campaigns, though some firms adopted a more cautious stance on the economic outlook,” he said.

See also: China LGFV says it can repay debt even as bond sale hits snag

Concerns over the health of the world’s second-largest economy have been intensifying since April as growth weakened and became more unbalanced. Top officials pledged to roll out “effective new policies in a timely manner” during a key policy meeting last week, but stopped short of introducing any fresh stimulus measures.

Investors are now looking to stimulus measures as Beijing targets an economic growth rate of 4.5% to 5% this year.

The private and official surveys cover different sample sizes, locations and business types, with the RatingDog report focusing on small and medium-sized firms.

See also: China Mobile said to be to mulling stake sale in Thailand’s True — Bloomberg

“The headline PMI plunge reflects a sharp cooling in domestic demand, but the underlying engine hasn’t stalled,” said Henry Hao, senior economist at Commerzbank AG in Singapore. “Resilient export activity, long-term backlog growth, and sustained job creation show that while the Chinese service sector is tapping the brakes, it is still expanding.”

title: Citigroup readies US$2 bil debt deal for KKR’s Integer buyout — Bloomberg
article:
(Aug 5): Citigroup Inc is leading preparations for a U$2.45 billion debt financing to support KKR & Co Inc’s acquisition of medical-device maker Integer Holdings, according to people familiar with the transaction.

The financing will comprise US$2.1 billion in funded debt in the form of a seven-year term loan and a US$350 million revolving credit facility that will be unfunded, said the people, who requested anonymity because the negotiations are private. In addition to Citigroup, Barclays Plc, UBS Group AG and Jefferies Financial Group Inc will also provide debt for the transaction.

A deal to sell the debt to investors in the US leveraged loan market could launch in September, they added, noting terms of the transaction are still under discussion and could change.

A representative for KKR declined to comment while Citigroup and Integer didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

KKR agreed to buy Integer on Monday in an all-cash deal valuing the company at about US$5.7 billion. Integer stockholders will receive US$127 per share under the terms of the deal that would take it private, the companies said.

For Citigroup, it’s the second time this year the US bank has nabbed a lead role for a medical-device developer. In January, the bank led an US$8.75 billion debt financing to support the roughly US$18 billion buyout of Hologic Inc, one of the largest leveraged buyouts this year.

See also: Fosun unit said to be near deal for Apollo-backed Athora Germany — Bloomberg

That deal comprised a US$7.25 billion leveraged loan that was priced at 2.25 percentage points over the US benchmark and a US$1.25 billion term loan A, Bloomberg News reported in January.

title: Temasek, Morgan Stanley eyeing Adtek pre-IPO investment — Bloomberg
article:
(Aug 5): Shenzhen Adtek Technology Co is close to raising up to two billion yuan (US$296 million or $380 million) in a private fundraising round ahead of its planned initial public offering (IPO) in Hong Kong, according to people familiar with the matter.

Singapore state investor Temasek Holdings Pte Ltd, Morgan Stanley’s private equity arm, and Asian investment firm CPE are likely to participate in the round, the people said, asking not to be identified because the deliberations are private.

The provider of optical connectivity products for data centres plans to use the proceeds to fund growth, the people said. Considerations are ongoing and no final decisions have been made, they said.

A representative for Adtek didn’t respond to a request seeking comment, while Temasek, Morgan Stanley and CPE declined to comment.

The pre-IPO round would serve as a stepping stone toward Adtek’s first-time share sale in Hong Kong. The company in May filed for an IPO in the city, adding to a wave of listings by Chinese companies related to data centres and artificial intelligence. It may seek to raise US$500 million ($640.43 million) or more and a valuation of US$3 billion to US$4 billion, people familiar with the matter have previously said.

Adtek was founded in 2007 and nine years later was named a National High-Tech Enterprise, its website shows. The company also has a factory in Vietnam.

See also: Startup founder buys Washington bank to extend fintech push

title: Singapore small and mid-caps narrow corporate governance performance gap with larger peers
article:
Small- and mid-cap (SMID) companies in Singapore have narrowed the corporate and transparency performance gap with large-cap companies in 2026, the latest Singapore Governance and Transparency Index (SGTI) found. The SGTI is conducted between CPA Australia, the Singapore Institute of Directors (SID) and the National University of Singapore (NUS).

The difference in mean scores between SMIDs and their larger peers came to 17.7 points this year, down from 19.8 points in 2025.

The SGTI 2026 scorecard takes into consideration three key parts: base scores, bonuses and penalties. Bonuses are awarded for exemplary corporate disclosures while penalties are applied on a company-specific, event-triggered basis. The index has taken a “dynamic assessment approach” since 2024 to “remain responsive to regulatory updates and evolving market expectations”. This means y-o-y scores should be “interpreted with care”.

Large caps are defined as companies with market capitalisation of above $1 billion each while SMIDs are seen as companies with market capitalisation of up to $1 billion each.

In the SGTI 2026, Keppel came in top in the general category, followed by ComfortDelGro, Jardine Cycle & Carriage, DBS and Sats.

The overall mean score stood at 69.5 points in the general category, down from 70.9 points in 2025. This year’s score comprised a mean base score of 62.4 points and a mean bonus of 11.1 points. This was offset by a mean penalty of 4.0 points.

See also: Visa to cut 7% of workforce as CEO seeks to revamp company

Despite the narrowed gap overall, the index found that large-caps still outperformed SMIDs across “key disclosure areas” with the largest gaps in disclosure and transparency, as well as ESG (environmental, social and governance) and stakeholders.

Large-caps achieved a mean normalised score of 67% in disclosure and transparency, 20 percentage points higher than the SMIDs. Large-caps also scored 79% in ESG and stakeholders, 13 percentage points higher.

This year, companies did well in disclosures related to rights of shareholders with a mean normalised score of 85%. This was followed by accountability and audit, and ESG and stakeholders with scores of 71% and 67% respectively.

See also: Australia regulator sends warning to auditors after KPMG scandal

According to the index, the top 100-ranked companies followed a similar performance pattern, while outpacing the overall mean score for disclosure and transparency by 16 percentage points. They also showed notably stronger results in ESG and stakeholders as well as accountability and audit.

CapitaLand Ascott Trust (CLAS) ranked first in the REIT and business trust category, followed by CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust (CICT), Netlink NBN Trust, CapitaLand Ascendas REIT (CLAR) and Far East Hospitality Trust (FEHT).

The overall mean score fell to 88.9 points this year compared to last year’s 90.2 points. This year’s score comprised a mean base score of 73.4 points, a mean bonus of 17.7 points and a mean penalty of 2.2 points.

Entities within the top 10 outperformed their peers by around 15 points on average, with a mean overall score of 104.3 points.

This year, REITs and business trusts exhibited strong performance in disclosures relating to rights of shareholders, with a mean normalised score of 97%. The mean scores for accountability and audit, and ESG and stakeholders were 87% and 78% respectively.

“Good governance is a cornerstone of investor confidence and sustainable business performance. Transparent and meaningful governance disclosures enable investors to make informed long-term decisions and strengthen trust in capital markets,” says Greg Unsworth, Singapore divisional president, CPA Australia.

“The results show that significant room for improvement remains in the corporate governance disclosures of SGX-listed companies. Strengthening these disclosures will help to deepen trust and investor confidence, which are important to sustaining the renewed vibrancy of Singapore’s capital market,” adds Professor Lawrence Loh, director of the centre for governance and sustainability at NUS Business School.

“Clear communication and transparency are key to helping companies unlock their true value. Companies must continue to strengthen their governance and disclosure processes so that investors can better understand their performance, prospects and long-term value,” says Yeoh Ooh Jin, SID chair.

title: US bans export of tungsten, battery waste to protect supplies
article:
(Aug 5): The US will ban exports of tungsten scrap and recycled battery materials from later this month, less than a week after President Donald Trump handed authorities power to keep potentially critical materials inside the country.

Suppliers of tungsten waste and black mass — a shredded form of metals from old lithium-ion batteries — will be required to sell domestically, although they can apply for exemptions, according to a rule published on the Federal Register. The restriction will remain in place for one year.

Trump last week signed a measure that allows officials to restrict exports of industrial waste containing critical minerals and materials, or CMMs. That’s part of a push to use the Cold War-era Defense Production Act to shore up supplies and reduce dependence on China.

“The President stated that the inadequate supply of CMMs poses an increasing risk to our national defence and security, and it is imperative that the United States take immediate action to secure the supply of recoverable CMMs,” the Department of Commerce said in the statement on the register.

Tungsten is a tough metal used in everything from military armour and ammunition to precision tools in car plants, and is among the cluster of metals subject to Chinese export controls. Black mass is made from recycled lithium-ion batteries and is a growing alternative source of lithium, cobalt, nickel and other materials.

title: GIC seeks to sell US$1 bil in private equity fund stakes — Bloomberg
article:
(Aug 5): Singapore’s GIC Pte Ltd is looking to offload some of its private equity stakes as the sovereign wealth fund taps the booming secondaries market to manage its investments, according to people familiar with the matter.

GIC is seeking to sell fund holdings with a net asset value of about US$1 billion ($1.28 billion), one of the people said, asking not to be identified as the discussions are private. The potential divestment includes funds from multiple global private equity managers, including EQT, TPG Asia and KKR & Co, some of the people said. PJT Partners is advising GIC on the deal, the people said.

The wealth fund reached out to potential buyers last month to gauge interest, the people added. The talks are at an early stage and details of any transaction could change, they said.

Representatives from GIC, PJT Partners, EQT and KKR declined to comment. TPG Asia wasn’t immediately able to comment.

GIC has become more cautious on private market investments and is actively “recycling” capital across such strategies, chief executive officer Lim Chow Kiat said in an interview last month. The wealth fund last month reported a 3.6% five-year annualized return, the lowest in more than a decade.

The secondaries market for private assets is booming as limited partners look to offload stakes before they mature and fund managers raise more capital in continuation vehicles to hold on to their prized or hard-to-sell assets for longer.

See also: Man Group assets hit all time high after bumper first half

Such transactions grew 19% from a year earlier to US$121 billion in the first half, according to Evercore Inc. Sales by limited partners were driven by large, repeat investors such as sovereign wealth funds, the report said.

GIC has US$1.16 trillion in assets under management, according to the latest estimate by Global SWF. Last year, the Singapore firm sought to sell private equity fund stakes with a net asset value of at least US$1 billion. In June, it finalised a separate sale of as much as US$2 billion of private credit assets.

title: Yen weakness a risk to US financial stability: DBS
article:
The recent, historic intervention by the US to support Japan’s ailing currency, the yen, arose from the threat a weak yen could pose to US financial stability, says DBS FX strategist Philip Wee.

In a note published on Aug 4, 2026, Wee writes that US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s call to expand the Federal Reserve’s Foreign International Monetary Authorities (FIMA) Repo Facility was not solely about addressing Japan’s domestic problems.

The FIMA program was established back in 2020 during the Covid-19 pandemic when borrowers were struggling to secure US dollars without liquidating their US Treasury holdings. FIMA allows foreign central banks to borrow US dollars against their holdings instead.

“As the world’s largest holder of US Treasuries, Japan could add pressure to elevated US bond yields,” Wee says. “The strategy appeared to have worked for now. The US Treasury 30-year yield eased for the first time in three sessions by 4.5 bps to 5.23% while the S&P 500 Index rose a third day by 1.5% to 7600.5 overnight.”

On July 31, 2026, the US and Japan mounted a joint intervention to stabilise the yen. The currency had been steadily depreciating amid a widening interest rate gap between Japan and other countries, as well as growing concerns over Japan’s weak fiscal position. Higher oil prices due to the ongoing war in Iran have also pushed Japan, a net importer of oil, to sell yen for the US dollar. The last time the US had intervened directly to support the yen was in 2011 following the Fukushima nuclear disaster.

According to Wee, the joint currency intervention will make it difficult for speculators looking to hold onto their short yen positions. Wee says the yen is now trading at around 157 to 158 per dollar, which more than offsets its spike to 160 to 164 per dollar after the Federal Reserve held rates steady at 3.5% to 3.75% following its meeting in June.

See also: Bessent says yen level problem for Japan, other currencies

“These speculators should also be mindful that the Japanese finance ministry is looking to boost demand for the JPY and JGBs (Japanese Government Bonds), including encouraging the country’s Government Pension Investment Fund to buy more domestic assets,” Wee writes in his note, noting that the US had reportedly sold euros instead of US dollars to support the yen.

“Apart from USD/JPY’s support level at 155, markets will also need to pay close attention to downside risks in the JPY carry trades, namely, the support levels for EUR/JPY at 180, and the one at 109 for AUD/JPY.”

title: Malaysia seeks to shield farmland from AI and chipmaking booms
article:
(Aug 5): Malaysia is working with state governments to protect farmland from industrial and real estate expansion as the explosive growth in data centres and chip manufacturing intensifies competition for land.

The Southeast Asian nation has already set aside about 25,000 hectares through the Permanent Food Production Zones programme, which will help protect land from encroachment by industries, said Deputy Agriculture and Food Security Minister Datuk Chan Foong Hin. That’s nearly 5% of Malaysia’s farmland, excluding palm oil and rubber plantations.

The ministry plans to propose expanding the area of protected arable land, he added, declining to specify by how much, or when the proposal would go to the Cabinet.

“We hope to maintain a certain percentage,” Chan said in an interview in Putrajaya, Malaysia’s administrative capital. “Especially, the current producing area should remain protected.”

Billions of dollars have flowed into data centres in Malaysia in recent years, with HSBC Holdings Plc estimating total investments amount to almost 18% of the country’s gross domestic product. The Southeast Asian nation has also emerged as a hub for manufacturing artificial intelligence hardware, ranking among the world’s four largest net exporters.

The breakneck growth has lured even the country’s palm oil giants into hosting server and solar farms on some of the vast tracts of land they control.

See also: Malaysia mulls easing rare-earth export curbs to meet global demand

There is growing “competition between industry and agricultural activities,” Chan said, adding that the state and local governments see data centres as more profitable or more advanced than agriculture. “That’s the dilemma.”

Land use is administered by local authorities and the federal government plans to align policies across states to strengthen food security, while remaining attractive to industry, Chan said.

Urbanisation is adding to the pressure on agricultural production. The sector’s share of Malaysia’s economy and employment has steadily declined over the past two decades, World Bank data show, sparking concerns about food security. Frequent global supply chain and climate disruptions have only heightened those worries.

See also: Anwar’s bloc loses control of another Malaysian state in setback

Land for livestock farming in particular has shrunk nearly 50% since 2017, pressured by infrastructure and urban growth, as well as non-food crops, according to a statement by Agriculture and Food Security Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Sabu in March. Malaysia’s farmland is dwarfed by plantations, mainly palm oil and rubber, which are mostly controlled by large companies.

“There is no simple answer and we have to show the government’s commitment to food security by creating the permanent food-producing areas,” Chan said.

title: DHLT reports lower 1HFY2026 DPU of 1.82 cents; flags higher financing costs ahead
article:
Daiwa House Logistics Trust has reported lower DPU of 1.82 cents for its 1HFY2026, as it suffered lower revenue and net property income due to higher portfolio occupancy and the effect of a weaker yen.

For the six months ended June, DPU was 18.8% lower y-o-y, revenue was down 11.8% to $25.7 mil, net property income down 13.4% to $19.5 million and distributable income down 18.5% to $12.8 million, mainly due to the lower NPI, higher interest expenses and lower realised exchange gains.

During the period, the yen weakened by 9.6% versus Singdollar, the reporting currency.

Despite this drop, DHLT says the long-term prospect of the logistics market in Japan is expected to be positive in general, as supply and demand dynamics rebalances.

Future supply of logistics space is expected to moderate amid rising construction costs while demand remains well supported by growing e-commerce.

Jun Yamamura, CEO of the manager, says he will continue to focus on improving the occupancy rate of the portfolio and thereby turn in a better performance.

See also: CLCT held up 1HFY2026 DPU at 2.45 cents despite softer economy and divestment

In 1HFY2026, DHLT renewed two leases with positive rent uplift while the occupancy rate of DPL Koriyama improved to 92.3% in July. Discussions on the vacant unit in DPL Kawasaki Yako are also progressing well.

"While the manager seeks to improve the occupancy of DPL Sendai Port, the manager is also concurrently exploring various options for DPL Sendai Port, including asset recycling," he adds.

DHLT warns that it has 12 billion yen of borrowings maturing towards the end of 2026, which were drawn during the period of negative interest rate environment in Japan.

See also: KIT to take 45% stake in second solar portfolio in Germany for $50 mi

Therefore, these borrowings will be refinanced at higher rates compared to their respective existing rates and DHLT's manager will take a balanced approach in terms of tenure of borrowings to manage the rate increase.

The first reset date of the perpetual securities is also this November.

"The weaker yen has also impacted DHLT’s results, although the manager noted a recent coordinated intervention by Japan and the US provided some reprieve to the yen.

"The manager will continue to adopt a disciplined and systematic hedging of JPY to mitigate volatility," says Yamamura.

DHLT units closed at 49 cents on Aug 4. It is down 12.5% year to date.
